parts.description: A cream-colored glazed ceramic bowl with a smooth rounded body, open circular rim, and small raised foot ring. The surface is glossy with subtle wear or discoloration near the rim.
parts.reasoning: The object appears to be a medium ceramic/porcelain bowl, roughly 12–14 cm in rim diameter and 6–8 cm tall, with a thin curved wall and a heavier base foot. A realistic total mass for this size of glazed ceramic bowl is about 0.35–0.50 kg; 0.42 kg is a suitable rigid-body estimate. The dominant structural/contact material is glazed ceramic, whose true material density is typically 2200–2600 kg/m^3, so 2400 kg/m^3 is used for the material density. Because the bowl is hollow, explicit mass should be authored rather than relying only on density times a convex collider volume, which would overestimate mass if the collider encloses the empty cavity. Glazed ceramic has moderate friction: lower than rubber or raw wood, but higher than glass on many dry surfaces. A static friction coefficient of 0.48 and dynamic friction coefficient of 0.36 are appropriate for a ceramic foot ring on common dry work surfaces. Restitution is kept modest at 0.32 because ceramic is hard but impacts are usually damped by the small contact patch, surface glaze, and lack of intentional elasticity; if fracture is not modeled, a low-to-moderate bounce prevents unrealistic lively behavior. The bowl is concave and open, so a single convex hull is physically wrong because it would cover the interior cavity. For best fidelity, an SDF mesh collider or a carefully built concave proxy should be used so objects can contact the inner surface. If performance is more important than exact interior contact, convex decomposition with multiple hulls around the wall and base is the preferred fallback. Small contact offsets around 2 mm are appropriate for this object scale in Isaac Sim/PhysX, with rest offset near zero to keep the visual ceramic surface aligned with collision response. CCD is recommended for drops or fast manipulation because the rim and wall are thin relative to possible velocities; otherwise it may be disabled for performance. Compliant contacts are not needed for a rigid ceramic bowl, but a very stiff, lightly damped contact model can be used if solver chatter occurs.
